subtopic: REPORTED LACK OF SEED AND FEED AT CARDROSS- DELAY IN DISTRIBUTION OF SEED WHEAT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REPORTED LACK OF SEED AND FEED AT CARDROSS- DELAY IN DISTRIBUTION OF SEED WHEAT
speechtext: I have been asked to bring to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) the fact that at Cardross, Saskatchewan, the farmers are without feed or seed; their horses have had no fodder since March, and it is alleged that they are without seed for the purpose of putting in a crop, although conditions seem to be favourable for an adequate return if they are fortunate enough to get the seed. I can only say that those who have asked me to bring the matter to the attention of the minister are of the opinion that if he will take notice of the conditions he may be able to remedy them.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: REPORTED LACK OF SEED AND FEED AT CARDROSS- DELAY IN DISTRIBUTION OF SEED WHEAT
speechtext: I would suggest that if those who send such telegrams would direct them to the provincial government they would get much more speedy action than by sending them around by way of Ottawa. I took this matter up fully with the government of Saskatchewan when I was in Regina last Friday and Saturday, and they are giving every attention to any delay that there may be in getting the seed grain distributed.

subtopic: REPORTED LACK OF SEED AND FEED AT CARDROSS- DELAY IN DISTRIBUTION OF SEED WHEAT
speechtext:
Apparently that action had been anticipated; for they complain that they are unable to get any action from Regina. That is the only reason it is brought to the attention of the minister through this channel at the moment. It is just possible, as

Member jor Beauce
it was Friday or Saturday that the matter was dealt with, and this telegram having come through Crane valley, that they were not aware of the conditions to which the minister has referred and to which I shall direct attention.

subtopic: REPORTED LACK OF SEED AND FEED AT CARDROSS- DELAY IN DISTRIBUTION OF SEED WHEAT
speechtext: I should like to direct the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to a report appearing in the two Regina newspapers, the Leader and the Star, to the effect that the Minister of Agriculture of that province had given an interview in which he stated that the wheat board was responsible for the delay. I understood that the federal minister was meeting with the wheat board in Winnipeg, or was getting in touch with them, and I was wondering if he would care to make a statement as to the result of that conference.

subtopic: REPORTED LACK OF SEED AND FEED AT CARDROSS- DELAY IN DISTRIBUTION OF SEED WHEAT
speechtext: I do not know whether I understood the first part of the remarks of the hon. gentleman. Was it suggested that I had made the statement that the wheat board was responsible?

subtopic: REPORTED LACK OF SEED AND FEED AT CARDROSS- DELAY IN DISTRIBUTION OF SEED WHEAT
speechtext: No. I have here the two Regina papers, which state that Mr. Taggart admits a hitch in distributing seed wheat, and charges the wheat board with responsibility for the delay. The report goes on to the effect that the federal Minister of Agriculture had been in communication with the wheat board by telephone, and it was understood that on his return to Ottawa he would take up the matter with the board in Winnipeg. I wondered if the minister cared to make a statement as to the result of that conference.

subtopic: REPORTED LACK OF SEED AND FEED AT CARDROSS- DELAY IN DISTRIBUTION OF SEED WHEAT
speechtext:
I interviewed the wheat board while passing through Winnipeg and also discussed the matter with the provincial government in Regina on Friday last:	In
those two interviews I discovered that there had been some delay due to the unnecessary sending of messages, first from Winnipeg to Regina and then from Regina back to Winnipeg, when the messages might have been transmitted from either one point or the other without the duplication that actually resulted. That probably brought about a delay of about one day in some of the distributions. The main difficulty in connection with distribution, however, is that this year wheat had to be found for a very large area, and had to be brought in from outside the province. Until very recently it was impossible to know the amounts that should be shipped to the different municipalities, but it is hoped that any delays will be overcome during the present week.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937

speechtext:
Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the second reading of Bill No. 80, respecting a certain trade agreement between Canada and Guatemala.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Agreement approved.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext:
We have had only a brief opportunity of glancing at this bill, which appears to be very ordinary and simple. The explanatory note indicates that it is an agreement providing for the exchange of most
2252	COMMONS
Canada-Guatemala Trade Agreement
favoured nation treatment. I should like to ask the minister whether, in the light of modern developments, or, shall I say, particularly developments in the older countries of Europe and indeed in all parts of the world, special consideration has been given recently by the government to the effect of the extension of most favoured nation treatment.
This is an old principle, as far as Canada is concerned, in international trade. If my memory serves me rightly, some twenty-two or twenty-three countries enjoy the privilege. I remember making an analysis a few years ago which indicated that whenever a reduction was given to one of these countries it extended also to the whole twenty-three countries. The result, of course, has been a much wider reduction in tariff charges than an individual agreement would indicate on its face, and I was led to the opinion that the whole system ought to be reviewed. When I say that I wish to assure the minister and the government that this observation is not offered in criticism of them or their policy, because this matter extends back over a number of governments and a great many years. But.in the light of changing conditions, with the controlled markets of many of these countries, it is a question whether we should continue the principle of extending in blanket form the most favoured nation treatment. I think I am within the judgment of the house and of those who have studied modern trade conditions when I say that in the last ten years the trend has been more to special agreements between countries, the limitation of imports except under quota arrangements, and such practices or customs as these would indicate, as against the blanket extension of all the privileges that are enjoyed by all these other countries, in this case to Guatemala. I am wondering whether or not we are wise in following that course. That is the question that arises in my own mind, and I was wondering if the minister had given any recent study to the situation and whether he would be prepared to-day to express an opinion as to the result of such study; also whether he considers the extension of most favoured nation treatment the best course to pursue in making new agreements with other countries.
Perhaps one further question might be asked: has he any opinion as to the wisdom of abrogating some of the existing treaties, again in the light of changed conditions? For instance, by the extension of the most favoured nation privilege we accord a country an extremely wide entry into our market. As a matter of fact, our general tariff might

be considered a dead letter to-day. Most stuff comes in under the intermediate tariff; I refer of course to other than British Empire countries. Therefore I feel strongly that the time has arrived when we should review conditions of import into each of these countries, the extent to which in recent years they have placed on imports restrictions which affect Canada as they affect other countries, and whether or not many of these countries are enjoying undue privileges with respect to the entry of goods into Canada under most favoured nation treaty arrangements as against the restriction of imports into their own markets.
Perhaps the minister will accept this somewhat casual way of expressing a difficult question and suggesting an important problem. I am quite sure he is familiar with the situation, and will grasp what I have very imperfectly put before him.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext:
As every hon. member knows, it is of course true that the conclusion of a most favoured nation agreement with any one country extends certain tariff privileges to all other countries with which we have most favoured nation arrangements. That it has worked to the detriment of Canada up to this point, I certainly would not like to say. As a matter of fact it is definitely the policy of this government to negotiate to promote the exchange of commodities with all countries. I would say, however, that when any agreement with any country whatsoever is contemplated, the specific interests of that country and their relation to Canada are very carefully considered before arrangements are made. So far as the agreements with Hayti and Guatemala are concerned, the implications are not important, because our trade with these countries is very small.
The former Minister of Trade and Commerce has asked whether or not the time has arrived to consider whether some of these agreements giving most favoured nation treatment should be cancelled or abrogated. That, again, is a question upon which I should not like to give a very definite opinion. Occasionally-and perhaps at the present time-it does happen that where we might desire to give certain concessions t-o one country we are obliged to hesitate because it would involve the same concessions to some other country, importations from which might be prejudicial to Canada. Speaking generally I believe it is in the interests of Canada and of the trading nations of the world to have as free an interchange of commodities as possible, without detriment to our own industries. In anticipation of some questions which might be asked may I say that the

Canada-Gualemala Trade Agreement
present bill involves the ratification of a trade agreement between Guatemala and Canada which was signed on September 28 of last year. It provides, as stated, for the exchange of most favoured nation treatment and- perhaps this will answer one question which has been asked-also that if either country introduces exchange restrictions, exchange control, a quota system or anything of the kind, Canada shall receive proportionately as good treatment as any other country.
The agreement is for three years, and will continue unless terminated by the giving of six months' notice. With regard to the point raised by the hon. member, as to whether or not we should consider abrogation, I would say offhand that it is not very probable. But where any agreements are made in which most favoured nation treatment is conceded to another country, the whole situation is carefully canvassed before the agreements are finally signed.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext: What is the volume of trade?

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext: Almost infinitesimally small. Last year the imports from Guatemala were valued at 852,000, of which all but $1,000 came in the form of coffee. The exports, consisting chiefly of wheat flour, amounted to only SS8.000.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext:
While the minister may say that the trade involved is small, I would remind him that the principle behind the treaty is not small. I suggest to him that in future not only treaties with smaller countries but also those with the United States be submitted to industrialists and agriculturists for study before bills are introduced. I suggest he should adopt a new policy, that followed by Right Hon. Neville Chamberlain and by the federal administration at Washington, of giving industrialists, agriculturists and others a chance to be heard before a treaty is consummated.
So far as these treaties are concerned, we are only having a post mortem. The agreements are signed, sealed and delivered. We have to swallow the whole thing, although some of our constituents may not favour the agreements which have been made. I do not object to the treaty now under consideration. But the government is running all over the world looking for treaties, while it forgets about the home market. I know that the present treaty is only a small one, and that a small amount of business is involved. I do point out however that we must consider an important principle, and must consider the effect agreements may have on employers of
labour and employees. We should not permit the making of treaties without first consulting the people interested and giving them a chance to be heard.
We are losing our home market, and prominent industrialists do not know where they stand. At Christmas time one may walk into Eaton's or Simpson's in Toronto and see on display the goods coming in under preferred treaties. From fourteen or fifteen countries we see goods of all descriptions, even down to Christmas cards, and all that sort of thing. This practice is taking the home market away from our own people. This is a stable market, not one which is here to-day and gone to-morrow. It is true that only a small amount of money is involved in this agreement, but an important principle must be considered, because we may have before us a treaty of greater importance, namely that between Great Britain and the United States. The British government have called industrialists and agriculturists to the city of London so that they may know what the government is doing. In Washington they have seen fit to send to Canada a list of forty-seven pages of items, and have asked their people to give consideration to them. Business men were to file their written objections or support by March 14. On March 20 there was a public hearing at Washington before which any person could express his views-not after the treaty was consummated, but before.
Coming from an industrial city I protest against the irregular practice of consummating treaties in this manner. It has been stated in the press that this is a decadent house. Someone should answer such a charge. I say the government should answer, but it has been left for a private member to do so. If this is a decadent house, I would say it is a decadent press which gives the public and business men no notice of treaties until they are consummated. The treaty with Hayti is to be considered, but we have had no notice of it. The press will print three or four pages of ballyhoo about sime kind -of sport, or that sort of thing, but not one line about these treaties.
The minister, who has some regard for the public, should consider a new policy. He should consider the possibility of giving business men proper legal notice. They should be given a chance to be heard and then there could be no complaints made. This is a matter of policy in administering this matter for Canada.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext:
The complaint made by my hon. friend arises out of the difference of
2254	COMMONS
Canada-Guatemala Trade Agreement
procedure in the two countries. I take it that he is referring to the United States, and, of course, to Canada. Under the law of the United States a certain procedure has to be followed by which a list of the articles in connection with which it is proposed to negotiate, with Canada in the present instance, must be published in order that the producers may be given an opportunity to make representations. That is not the procedure followed in Canada. As to whether that should be done would be a matter for future consideration by the government. My hon. friend is in error when he states that the same practice was followed in connection with the treaty with Great Britain. They did not follow the policy of notifying their industrialists to come in and make representations.
I am not so sure that any great practical benefit would result if the industrialists were called in in advance. I am quite sure my colleague, the Minister of Finance, will bear me out when I say that practically every producer and manufacturer in Canada has already made representations with regard to every commodity under the sun in connection with which we may negotiate with the United States. Any trade agreement which we might make with the United States will have to be ratified later on by parliament, at which time a full discussion can take place.
I think it should be stated that where we make a most favoured nation arrangement with another country, Great Britain and all the other parts of the empire are excluded from the operation of that clause. In connection with this particular treaty with Guatemala, the other Central American republics are excluded from the operations of the most favoured nation clause.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext: What countries are they?

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext: I am not sure that I can enumerate them. It is all the Central American republics, and they can be easily identified. As far as Hayti is concerned, the exception there applies to the Dominican republic, which is a part of the same island.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext: Is it expected that these treaties will greatly increase our trade with these countries?

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext:
I would not care to make any prediction with regard to that. Having regard to all the circumstances, I do not suppose it is physically possible that our trade with either of these two countries will ever be very large. However, it has been thought well to make this trade agreement because of certain restrictions which might be brought into force

with reference to exports from Canada to Guatemala if no regular agreement were made.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext: What are the transportation facilities for the exchange of trade between Canada and Guatemala?

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext: I am not sure that I can give an answer to that question. They would probably consist of tramp steamer service which would be offered from time to time, as well as rail facilities.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext: Are the Central American republics specified in the agreement?

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext: I do not think they are mentioned.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext:
They are named. Article IX reads:
The advantages now accorded or which may hereafter be accorded by Guatemala to the commerce of Costa Rica, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua or Panama, so long as any such advantage is not accorded to any other country shall be excepted from the operation of this agreement.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext: Is this treaty designed to give assistance to any particular commodities which it is hoped Canada will be able to export or import?

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext: As I said before, we have not any great hope that our trade is going to be considerably extended. However, we hope to keep what we have. I could give the names of the commodities which we now sell, but in most instances the amounts are quite small.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext: What about mahogany and woods of that kind?

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext: For importation into Canada?

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext: I said exports or imports.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext: I do not know that any particular commodity has been kept in mind Like most countries, we are more concerned perhaps with exports than with imports. We export wheat flour, rubber tires and tubes, various vegetable products, newsprint, rubber belting, silk socks and stockings, brushes, cotton duck, farm implements, bags, whisky, cotton cloth, needles and pins, and other commodities, but in most cases the amounts are quite small.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext:
Article IV, which I believe is a little unusual, reads:
In the event that the government of Canada or the government of Guatemala establishes or maintains an official monopoly or centralized agency for the importation of or trade in a particular commodity, the government establishing or maintaining such monopoly or centralized agency will give sympathetic consideration to all representations that the other government may make with respect to alleged discriminations against its commerce in connection with purchases by such monopoly or centralized agency.
In the absence of precise knowledge of the origin of that article it would appear that there is either already in existence or contemplated a centralized agency or monopoly in connection with some article of commerce that is likely to enter into trade between the two countries. Instead of the agreement specifically undertaking that Canada shall have fair treatment by such centralized agency or monopoly, all that is done is to assure that sympathetic consideration will be given to representations made. Sympathetic or courteous consideration is usually accorded to any friendly country, so that in a treaty of this kind these words are meaningless. On the other hand, the article seems to imply the existence of a monopoly. The minister mentioned coffee, and it may be that the export of coffee from Guatemala is controlled. It also may be possible that some article entering that country from Canada is at present under government monopoly-we will say, for instance, flour, which might indeed be an important article of export. If it were under the control of a central monopoly in Guatemala, then such central agency could very well discriminate, and this agreement would not ensure to Canada either most favoured
nation treatment or any treatment at all except such as the monopoly might desire to give us.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext: There is a clause which declares that Canada shall not be discriminated against in any case such as that. For instance, if exchange control or a quota were imposed by Guatemala she could not do it to the disadvantage of Canada as compared with any other country.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext:
I am quite aware of
that, blit the very presence of this article implies that some central agency does exist, or else the article is superfluous.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext:
I will give another reason
for that.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext:
Frankly, I think the
article is one that should not be in the agreement, but of course it is there and I suppose we must accept it, and that is all there is to it. But I was wondering if the minister had the facts behind it, because there must be something behind this article. It strikes me that there is a central agency or a number of central agencies controlling, we will say, imports; buying, we will say, all the flour, all the lumber or some other commodity and supervising its distribution within that territory. That is quite a common practice nowadays in many countries, and if such exists then it might well nullify the effects of this treaty, because that does not affect the question of exchange or import quotas or matters of that kind. These are governmental actions. But this contemplates the establishment or the actual existence of an official monopoly or central agency. I think some explanation of that should be given to the committee.

maintopic: CANADA-GUATEMALA TRADE APPROVAL OF AGREEMENT SIGNED ON SEPTEMBER 28, 1937
speechtext:
It is covered by the agreement itself. The monopoly covers matches, wax matches and lighters, and it is so indicated in article II, in the last paragraph, which is the reason for article IV being in the agreement. Article II says:
The advantages and provisions contained in the present article and in article IV shall not be applicable to the importation, production or sale of matches, wax matches and lighters, in view of the existing laws in Guatemala on the monopoly of such goods.
>
And article IV sets out the matter in the terms there indicated.
I cannot understand why there is nothing in this schedule that indicates who made it. It is the first time I can recall such a thing happening, although I am not challenging my memory with it. This is an agreement purporting to be made between two countries.

Trade Agreement between Canada and Guatemala
The government of Canada and the government of Guatemala, desiring to further facilitate and develop the commercial relations existing between Canada and Guatemala, have resolved to conclude a trade agreement and for this purpose have agreed upon the following articles:
And at the close we have these words:
In witness whereof, the undersigned, duly authorized to that effect, have signed the present agreement and have affixed their seals hereto.
Done at Guatemala City, this twenty-eighth day of September nineteen hundred and thirty-seven, in duplicate in English and Spanish, both texts being equally authentic.

There is nothing to indicate who these people are. The minister now tells me that one of them is the British consul. I do not know who the other, Carlos Salazar, is. There must be some reason why an agreement submitted to this parliament for confirmation does not indicate who the parties are who signed it. Any agreement that I have ever seen made with any community, however small, usually states that it is made between the government of the country represented by so-and-so. One of the agreements we made with the West Indies was signed by five or six of their ministers, and it was stated who they were on the face of the agreement.

A number of the Canadian life companies which do business in the United Kingdom and in other parts of the world have asked that we take cognizance of the fact that, particularly in Great Britain, new types of public authorities have come into being. As it was originally, the limitation would be to a body responsible to the government of such kingdom or dominion, or to any minister of such government; whereas in many such cases there are bodies which are responsible to the minister, which in turn occupy a regulatory relationship to the body actually issuing the securities. So the insertion of these words will make it clear that if the body is under government supervision and control, then the bonds of such public utility or other corporation would be a proper investment for Canadian life insurance companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932, AS TO INVESTMENT OF FUNDS
speechtext:
The difficulty there is due to the fact that the body may not be a

Natural Resources
governmental body in the ordinarily accepted sense of the term. It may be a body administering a utility-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932, AS TO INVESTMENT OF FUNDS
speechtext: -but under a board which in turn is under the direction of the minister. We are endeavouring to include the various types of quasi-governmental authorities which are being erected in England particularly, which are nevertheless public in reality. The law officers have had some difficulty in finding descriptive terms which would cover specific cases which have been put up to the department, as, for instance, the electricity board, the Port of London Authority, the London Transport Board, all of which have in varying degrees relationship with a minister of the crown of Great Britain. In some cases that relationship is direct; they are immediately under the minister's direction with respect to rates and matters of that sort; in other cases they are responsible to a board which reports to the minister, the board itself in most cases being a board of civil servants, in some cases with what are called over there co-opted members. Various experiments are taking place in England of a very interesting nature with respect to the combination, in the operation of great public utilities particularly, of private enterprise on the one hand and governmental capital investment or supervision, or both, on the other. You cannot use a phrase which is descriptive of all these experiments, because they vary in certain particulars. But there is no doubt that the securities issued by them rank very high in England, and it is for that reason that we think Canadian insurance companies, particularly those doing business in England, should have the right to invest in such securities, which in England are regarded as being prime securities.

subtopic: CONFIRMATION OF CERTAIN AGREEMENTS BETWEEN DOMINION GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES OF MANITOBA, SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA

speechtext:
Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to confirm certain agreements between the government of the dominion and the governments of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, respectively, concerning the transfer to the said provinces of the interest of the crown, in the right of the dominion, in and to certain natural resources.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONFIRMATION OF CERTAIN AGREEMENTS BETWEEN DOMINION GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES OF MANITOBA, SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this resolution will authorize the introduction of a bill to confirm amendments to the agreements transferring the natural resources of the three western provinces. They were transferred under agreements which mentioned that all lands, mines and minerals in the right of the crown were to be transferred to the respective provinces. There has been doubt as to whether those terms included waters and water powers, and in order to remove the doubt an additional agreement has been signed with the three provinces transferring waters and water powers as well. That was always the intention, and this is merely to avoid any difficulty in that regard.

subtopic: CONFIRMATION OF CERTAIN AGREEMENTS BETWEEN DOMINION GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES OF MANITOBA, SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA
speechtext:
Are any regulations included in these agreements with regard to natural resources? For instance, one of the agreements is with Alberta, where there are valuable oil and coal deposits. From some of the factums and briefs which have been presented to the Rowell commission we have
Natural Resources

learned how the natural resources of this country have been squandered. I believe the time has come when we should have some regulation in this regard, because one of these days the United States are not going to have enough coal for their own people, let alone enough for us. I believe these provinces, especially the three prairie provinces, since they are the only ones left where such regulations could be enforced, should be under some sort of control with regard to their natural resources in order that these resources may be conserved for the future. In the old province of Ontario we have had trouble about water power. They will have it in this resolution without riders. In Canada we have 42,000,000 horse power in all, but only one-seventh of it has been developed. So I believe there should be some provision in these statutes for federal authority and conservation in this regard.
At the present time federal authority in Canada is the weakest it has been since confederation. There seems to be no central control over these provinces. We have agreements made both without and within the British North America Act. If there is one thing this country needs at the present time it is cohesion and unity between the provinces, but to-day they are like a lot of Balkan states, quarrelling among themselves and fighting federal authority. No doubt the resolution will pass, but when the bill is brought down I hope the minister will consider inserting some provision for the protection of posterity by conservation of natural resources. This country does not belong to those who inhabit it to-day. It is an inheritance from the past, a possession for the present and a trust for the future. Notwithstanding the reflections that have been cast on this House of Commons, this body is quite competent to deal with the affairs of the country without appointing royal commissions. If we hand over all these great natural resources in these provinces, oil, coal and all the rest of it, without restriction, we shall be criticized by posterity. We have seen the trouble the British government has had in Mexico in regard to oil. Here in Canada in Alberta we have the Turner valley, and as I stated when I first came to this house, we should have a national policy dealing with all our resources, including coal, oil, lumber, water powers and so on.
There should be some measure of protection and of conservation. It may be said that under the British North America Act we have that protection as to cash subsidies. Each year we hand over to the provinces certain sums of money by way of cash subsidies, but when it comes down to the fine point we have

absolutely no control over these subsidies, although they arise under the British North America Act. The provinces spend the money as they wish, though it was intended for provincial and municipal purposes. This is the only way in which we can bring to the attention of this parliament the need, from social, economic and business standpoints, of doing something to protect these resources in these interprovincial agreements. In British Columbia they are selling timber to Japan, I am told, for about $1.30 a thousand. It costs $10 to deliver it in Toronto by the Panama canal. I am not in the lumber business, and I have not my papers here, but that resource is being squandered to-day. In England and other countries they are doing something to put a brake on conservation of resources and on this sort of thing, but here it is almost too late. In the United States the federal government is trying to exercise some control over the states.
These three provinces in this resolution are as rich in natural resources as any provinces of Canada. The Lord did not intend these wonderful natural resources to be only for the millionaires who can take a holiday once in a while in Bermuda or the West Indies. The Lord intended the water power, coal, oil and all the rest of our great resources for the benefit of all his creatures, not for the few favoured people of this country. That is the trouble to-day. In a rich country like Canada, with all the natural resources that we possess, we have people suffering and starving in a land of plenty though we have all the fuel and oil we need and all the falling water to generate power to help the poor farmers who are struggling on the land. This is a very important bill; as I have said many times before, we should have a legal committee where matters of this kind can be considered. In my opinion there should be some rider inserted in the statutes which will protect the people of the country and establish some federal authority.

speechtext:
As I explained in the discussion on the resolution preceding the

introduction of the bill, the measure is introduced to extend for a further period of ten years the present provisions of the act with respect to the national battlefields commission.

subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF
subsubtopic: $75,000 A YEAR FOR PERIOD NOT EXCEEDINQ TEN YEARS
speechtext:
The national battlefields park is a dominion memorial. There has been considerable discussion lately in Quebec city with regard to a move to place in the park a new' monument which has no connection with the purposes for which this memorial was created. I have had correspondence with several individuals in Quebec who have urged that the commission cannot be said to be carrying out its trust when it permits the battlefields park to be used in this way. It seems that recently an American lady offered to donate a statue of Joan of Arc which it is proposed to place in this park. Many people feel that this statue should not be placed on what is a Canadian historic site. I believe the case is fairly well put in an editorial which appeared in the Quebec Chronicle-Telegraph of March 25, a paragraph of which reads as'follows:
Under these circumstances, the chairman and members of the commission, although it happens that most of them at present are residents of Quebec city, are trustees for the whole nation and are not justified in acting from any merely provincial or parochial point of view'. It will hardly be pretended, for instance, that public opinion in Canada desires or would approve of the use of the park for the erection of monuments having no connection with Canadian history and of direct interest only to some particular section or group of the population.
I5y what process of reasoning, then, the commissioners can reconcile it with their duty to accept a monument of St. Joan of Arc from a private individual who is an alien citizen and resident, and erect it as a conspicuous feature of the park, we are at a loss to think.
The editorial goes on to state that an appeal has been made in vain to the commissioners with regard to this matter. I think it is only fair that the matter should be introduced into this discussion and the minister give an explanation as to why this action should be taken.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT TO COMMISSION OF
subsubtopic: $75,000 A YEAR FOR PERIOD NOT EXCEEDINQ TEN YEARS
speechtext:
At a former stage of the discussion of this matter I was asked certain questions by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps). I have also received communications from various organizations. No application had been made by the commission for authority to erect anything of this nature and consequently it was necessary to make inquiries. I do not think I can do better by way of explanation than read a letter which I received from Sir George Gameau, who has been chairman of this commission for

Battlefields Commission
thirty years. The letter is addressed to me under date of March 29, 1938, and reads:
I was informed of the debate which recently took place in the House of Commons when you moved that the house go into committee of supply to consider the resolution authorizing the payment to the commission of the sum of $75,000 a year, for a period not exceeding ten years from April the 1st, 1938.
Having read most carefully in Hansard the questions asked and answers given during this short debate, I feel it advisable to inform you immediately of the particulars concerning the valuable gift of a bronze statue of Joan of Arc; the work and conception of one Anna Hyatt Huntington, officer of the Legion of Honour; and offered and given to the commission by Mr. and Mrs. Archer Milton Huntington, of New York.
Acting under the terms of its charter, the commission gratefully accepted this donation; which being a gift entailing no expenditure did not, in our opinion, necessitate the approval and sanction of the governor general in council.
Were it not for the questions put to you recently before the house, I would have waited until a later date to acquaint you, in greater detail, of all that had transpired in the matter.
This equestrian statue of Joan of Arc, one and a half times life size, is the replica of those already erected at Blois, in France, and at Riverside Drive, in New York.
The offer of this statue was made to us in the first days of August, 1937. The gift comprised not only the statue, but its pedestal and base, as well as the expense of erecting it.
The donation was accepted by the commission at its meeting held on September the 2nd, and I then proposed the sunken garden as the most suitable place to erect the statue; as here it would enhance the beauty of the garden, without being directly connected with the historical portion of the park.
This sunken garden occupies a strip of land 540 feet by 140 feet. It is bordered on one side by Laurier avenue, a city street, and on the other by No. 1 driveway of the park. Being long and narrow, it has proved difficult to treat along the lines used in landscaping the rest of the park. The placing of the statue in this section would solve the difficult problem of decoration, and meet in part objections raised in certain quarters as to the advisability of erecting, in the battlefields park, the statue of a personage not connected with Canadian history.
It was with this object in view, and in the hope of eliminating all such controversy, that we made the choice of this site.
A meeting of the board was called on December the 17th when the commission, after due consideration of all factors concerned, resolved to maintain its previous decision and accept this munificent gift to the people of Canada.
The suggestion has been made that the Montcalm monument be removed from its present position and placed in the sunken garden and that this vacant site be occupied by the statue of Joan of Arc. This, in our opinion, would be quite unsuitable, as the small size of the Montcalm monument would be further dwarfed by the large area in which it would stand.
51952-144}
I confess that I fail to see how the erection of this statue can detract from the historical significance of the park. Joan of Arc died over 300 years before the conquest of Canada and her statue symbolizes the valour and patriotism of the men of 1759 and 1760, which we commemorate in the park.
My long association with the development of the battlefields park, covering as it does a period of thirty years may I hope give the assurance that in the opinion I have reached with my colleagues we have been moved only by the desire to accomplish satisfactorily the work entrusted to us; and, in the fulfilment of this duty, we have endeavoured to give to those who so generously contributed to this park a memorial worthy of our country.
I thought it well to place on record Sir George Garneau's answers to the questions asked when this matter was before the house on a previous occasion. Perhaps I could summarize by saying that the statue is being donated and will cost the national battlefields commission nothing; they will not even have to pay the cost of erection. As Sir George Garneau points out, the statue is not being placed in what might be termed the historic part of the battlefields park; in fact, it will be nowhere near the actual battlefield. It is to be placed just off one of the main streets of Quebec which borders the battlefield and will be between that street and number one driveway which gives access to the battlefield. After reading Sir George Garneau's letter I felt that no valid objection could be made to the acceptance by the commission of this gift and its erection in the particular spot to which it had been assigned.

a figure of historic interest in that connection, but I have such confidence in Sir George Gameau that when he states, as he does in this report, that the statue is not to be erected on the historic battlefields site but in another portion altogether, so that the purport of its erection may not be misunderstood, it satisfies me and I think will satisfy the house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext: Is the minister going to speak on this bill?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext: Oh yes, in committee.

speechtext: Not unless I find it necessary.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext:
I was waiting to give the
minister the courtesy to speak. I wish to say something. As the subject of this bill deals entirely with waters that lie off the district I represent, and nobody else, I think, handles it, it behooves me to take some interest in the matter, and in the past I have done so.
The purport of the bill might be best expressed by referring to the explanatory note on page 2. I may preface that by saying that the pelagic sealing treaty was enacted between the United States, Britain, Japan and Russia-Canada was a contributor by virtue of being at that time under the British government-in 1911, forbidding pelagic sealing except to some stated Indians under certain conditions. The explanatory note says this:
The legislation adopted at the time-the Pelagic Sealing Act-contains no provision whereby such Indian or other aborigine could be penalized for violating this provision of the treaty.
I have read that explanation with a great deal of interest and pleasure, because I have been trying to tell the officials of the department that for the last nine months, and they have been sedulously denying it; and now,
CMr. Rinfret-.l
I think with admirable frankness, they have stated it in the explanatory note. The matter arises in this way. I will not go into details, but some man or some company with a very obvious axe to grind made representations to the government here that certain Indians were fishing illegally on the Pacific ocean, and the department in my humble opinion got stampeded and at once issued a most peremptory and, I think, ill-considered order that all skins were to be seized by the customs officers-who do not know anything about seals-provided not that they showed evidence of having been taken illegally, but that, they showed evidence of having been shot. There was a great deal of correspondence between the department and myself. The minister very kindly-and I now express my gratitude to him for doing so-gave permission and arranged that a case should be taken before the exchequer court. It is now before the court or in process of being brought there, so, the matter being sub judice, I will not go any further with the merits of that particular case.
As regards the bill itself, as amended it contains fourteen sections, but I fail to see that it leaves the matter very much clearer than it was to start with. I take exception more particularly to section 4, which says:
The governor in council may make such regulations as may be deemed necessary for the purpose of carrying out the convention or for giving effect to any of its provisions.
That of course is a clause such as we find in many bills, but I do not think we find it under conditions such as depicted here; because whoever has the power to make these regulations is not going to make regulations, he is going to make a law. The whole purport of this bill is to put restrictions and penalties on Indians breaking the law in that regard. It is all going to be left to regulations made by the government; they may be wise or unwise, reasonable or unreasonable, but once made they are there, and the act says they shall have the full force of law. In a matter where the very purpose of the bill is concerned it is going to be done by regulation. I submit the greater features at least should be expressed in the bill itself.
Then we come to the other sections. They do not seem to agree. Section 5 says that anyone who breaks the treaty "shall be guilty of an offence against this act". Section 6 says something different. It says that if any person other than an Indian, etc., uses

Pelagic Sealing
a port or equips a vessel with the idea of going sealing illegally, he shall be liable to a fine, but does not state the amount.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext: Pardon me; there will be an amendment to that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext:
That is what I was wanting to hear; I thought the minister would explain it was a mistake. It "was in the old act, but that it was wrong twenty-five years ago does not make it any better now. But under that section he will be liable to a fine or two years' imprisonment upon indictment, or on summary conviction to imprisonment or fine. This is what he is liable to get, on summary conviction, which means conviction before two justices of the peace, not sitting as police magistrates in a city, but away out in the bush on the Pacific coast, men who have been selected very often because it is necessary to have someone to sign papers and not for their legal knowledge or training. On summary conviction by two justices of the peace an offender will be liable to a penalty of 8500-no minimum, and I know justices of the peace who have the idea that the maximum fine should always be imposed. The maximum is $500, and six months' imprisonment, no minimum; and further, the vessel and everything connected with it is liable to seizure and forfeiture. That is the result of committing an ordinary offence against the act. And the people who come under it, by virtue of section 5, and section 8 where Indians are concerned, are liable.
Here is the discrepancy: I direct the attention of the Minister of Justice to section 6, which provides a penalty, as I have already indicated, for anyone equipping a boat with the intention of going sealing. But subsection 2, which I think should apply to the whole lot, reads as follows:
If any officer authorized by the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act to board and search is satisfied that there is reasonable cause for believing that a vessel has been or is being equipped contrary to this section, he may seize and detain the vessel and bring her for adjudication before the Exchequer Court of Canada on its admiralty side, or before any superior court in the province in or near which the vessel was seized.
(3) The court may thereupon adjudge the vessel and her equipment to be forfeited to His Majesty. . . .
There is the difference. If a poor ignorant Indian goes out and takes a seal in the open sea in pursuance of immemorial custom he is liable to have his little boat and gear and everything he possesses seized and forfeited, not on the adjudication of the exchequer court, in which we all have the greatest confidence,
but on the mere say-so of an officer as defined under the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act, which includes a fisheries officer. A fisheries officer is a man in the employ of the fisheries department, he may have been there only two weeks; he may be a political hack of the most obvious description and owe his appointment to that cause, but he has this power. I do not care what act it is in; I contend it is wrong, and that n-o one short of a court should have the power to declare the forfeiture of something on sight.
A clear case occurred two years ago in my own district in connection with the fisheries regulations. There was one of these absurd- I think I should rather call them infamous- sections, by which a man's boat worth perhaps $15,000 could be confiscated on sight by a fisheries officer. The man was charged with some comparatively trivial offence, such as fishing illegally in a certain place. The fisheries officer was told about it and went and seized his boat. It was quite illegal, because he had to do it on sight, and it was not done on his sight but someone told him of it. Before the case came up for trial- for there was a charge as well-someone enlightened the fisheries officer as to his error and he withdrew the confiscation. The man went on trial and was acquitted; he was pronounced innocent of any offence, yet if that fisheries man had happened to see the boat the seizure would have been legal and condemnation and forfeiture to the crown would have been legal. So we should have had the remarkable and utterly unjust situation of a man charged with an offence against the law, properly tried and legally acquitted, and yet unable except by mercy of the crown to get back his boat which had been seized.
The same thing exists here. It may be a case of a wealthy firm equipping a schooner; the boat can be seized by one of these subordinates, and that is all right, but he cannot condemn it; he can only bring it before the nearest exchequer court or superior court. But under section 8 this wretched Indian is liable to have everything he owns in the world forfeited on the say-so of someone who is described as a fisheries official. I submit it ought to go before a court in every case; let the man be prosecuted and brought into court, and let the forfeiture follow conviction. But to have a condition under which it would be possible for an innocent man to be acquitted but his boat previously forfeited is utterly intolerable. Section 8 says that the Indian who fishes illegally can have his boat seized by any officer authorized to board and search, and it shall be forfeited to his majesty.

Pelagic Sealing
That ought to be followed by the words "after due process of law" or something of the kind.
I have already referred to the severe penalty. You never make law good by making the penalties too severe. In almost every other act in connection with summary convictions you find-the Minister of Justice will correct me if I am wrong-that there is a minimum penalty provided so as to prevent ignorance or personal feeling operating to give a man a tremendous penalty, perhaps $500, for shooting a seal the skin of which may be worth $2.50.
Then section 5 provides that an Indian is not subject to the act if he has been engaged in pelagic sealing in convention waters in strict compliance with the stipulations of article 4 of the convention. Let us look at article 4. It says that:
It is further agreed that the provisions of this convention shall not apply to Indians, Ainos, Aleuts, or other aborigines dwelling on the coast of the waters mentioned in article I who carry on pelagic sealing in canoes not transported by or used in connection with other vessels, and propelled entirely by oars, paddles, or sails, and manned by not more than five persons each, in the way hitherto practised and without the use of firearms.
Now there is a contradiction in law, and certainly in common sense. It was put in there by the British when they were drawing up the treaty nearly twenty-five years ago, and were not familiar with conditions on the Pacific coast and ocean. They drew it up wrongly. It says, "a way hitherto practised and without the use of firearms." I submit that the one contradicts the other, because the old way did permit the use of firearms. There is no question about that. I am thoroughly familiar with the subject; I lived there for many years; I was Indian agent and had to do with these Indian crews and sailing captains, and I have often heard them talk about it.
The course followed by the sealers was this: They used to be fitted out in Victoria in the early spring, probably in March. Then they went down the California coast and came up there. Very often they ran into Victoria to get fresh stores, and then proceeded up towards Bering sea, going up the west coast of Vancouver island. That is where they took the skins now in dispute, but for all that distance from the California coast up to Bering sea they were allowed to use shotguns. There is no question about that. They did not always do so; if they could use their speara they preferred to do so, since a seal that is shot is liable to sink.
(Mr. Neill.]

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext: Might I ask the hon. member whether they were allowed the use of shotguns when the treaty was signed in 1911, forbidding the use of firearms?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext:
Yes, they were. The business had dwindled so much that there was very little done, but they were allowed the use of firearms outside Bering sea. When they reached that point the American or Canadian cutter came up and compelled them to seal their guns. If the guns had been illegal all along the cutter would not have sealed them up; it would have seized them, but they were allowed the use of firearms as far as Bering sea. Now the words are "as hitherto practised." If that is to be the policy they can use firearms now. If the intention had been to introduce something different from the existing practice they would have said "hitherto practised but without the use of firearms." They did not say "but"; they said "and," indicating that they thought there were no guns allowed on the coast at all. That was a mistake; the wording was erroneous, and it should be corrected now. There is provision under the treaty for conferences by means of which the various signatory governments can get together and agree on modifications of the treaty, and I believe that should be done. In any case I maintain that these Indians are entitled to go out and use a gun off the coast of Vancouver island, because that was the old way of getting the seals.
What was that provision put in the treaty for? The idea was that these were poor, uneducated Indians, unable to earn their living other than in the ways to which they were accustomed, and it was considered desirable to perpetuate the status quo and let them go on doing what they had been doing befqre. That is all I am asking. The language is capable of being interpreted in the other way, I admit, but I believe it should be interpreted according to what was evidently the intention of the framers of the legislation.
There is another point I should like to make; perhaps it is not quite so strong as this but still I think it is applicable. This treaty was negotiated twenty-seven years ago. At that time the idea was to rehabilitate the sealing industry, which had fallen to a very low level, owing to the methods of sealing in practice and the frequent poaching that went on. Sealing was practically nonexistent, and it was considered desirable to get together and draw up this treaty so that the herd could be built up. That was why they restricted the Indians to the old method.

Pelagic Sealing
But those conditions no longer exist, and I think we should move with the times and allow the Indians the same facilities we allow anyone else, twenty-seven years after the event. The seal herds have increased enormously under this protection, so much so that they are becoming a menace to salmon fishing on the Pacific coast. I have heard many .people advocate that we denounce the treaty altogether and begin to kill the seals in the old way because of the enormous number of salmon they eat. Of course people who want to prove the opposite catch a few seals at a time and place when they know there are no salmon in the water. Then they triumphantly produce the stomachs of the seals and say, "These seals are not eating salmon; there are none in their stomachs." Of course there would not be any, because there were no salmon for them to eat. I remember an argument one time in regard to sea lions; it was said that only seaweed had been found in their stomachs, and it was argued that therefore they lived on seaweed. I suppose if they had found a piece of motor tire in the stomach of a sea lion they would have argued that they lived on motor tires; and that would have been possible, because old motor tires are used as fenders on many of the fishing boats.
I submit that there is no longer need to protect the seals, and that is an additional reason why we should not be too hard on the Indian. Then again, why should we not allow the Indian to use modern methods? In 1922 a royal commission consisting of members of this house went thoroughly into conditions on the Pacific coast. We found that on the Skeena river no one, white or Indian, was allowed .to use a power boat. A fisherman was not allowed to have a little Evin-rude or a little two horse-power engine to buck the tide; he had to use sails or oars. It seemed an extraordinary thing that people who were licensed to go fishing should not be allowed to do so in the most modern and appropriate manner. On investigation we discovered that the reason was purely a financial one. At that time the canners financed those people much more than is the case at present, and they foresaw that they would be up against buying engines for all these boats. So they violently objected to the use of engines, but we could not see that it was unreasonable or improper that a man who was licensed to catch salmon, who was restricted by closed hours, seasons and so forth, should be allowed to catch the fish in the most practical method possible. Therefore we ordered that they should be allowed to use power boats thereafter, and nothing in particular happened except that it was a great deal more convenient for the fishermen. I suppose going back to antiquity we can recall that members of parliament, if they existed in those days, used to blot their letters with sand instead of using blotting paper, and they made copies of everything by hand, just as the monks did, some of whom would spend half a lifetime writing one book. We do not need to do such things now; we have gone ahead with the times, and if we allow the Indian to catch seals I do not see why he should not do it in the most reasonable way and with the least effort possible.
As I mentioned before, article 16 of the treaty contains a provision whereby one or more of the parties concerned may ask for a conference forthwith between representatives of all parties to consider and agree upon a further extension of the convention with such conditions and modifications, if any, as may be considered desirable. So there is opportunity for this government, in agreement with the other nations concerned, to make such modifications as would meet the situation, without going to the extent of entirely denouncing the treaty. I submit that in fairness to these Indians that should be done. They are not represented by members here, but because they do not have members representing them they should not be penalized. In New Zealand, where there is a comparable race called the Maoris, they have four members to represent them in parliament, so their interests are well looked after. We should not discriminate against the Indian here. A white man who has a schooner and who proposes to go out sealing illegally cannot have his vessel seized until the matter has been disposed of by the exchequer court, but in the case of the poor Indian his vessel may be seized on the mere say-so of a man calling himself a fisheries officer.
I do not submit these views to the department in any spirit of antagonism at all, but, I do hope they will consider these points when they are dealing with this matter later on.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext:
As indicated in the
explanatory note, this bill is for the purpose of amplifying a measure passed in 1913 which was passed in confirmation of the treaty entered into and signed in 1911 by Great Britain, the United States, Japan and Russia, regulating sealing in Pacific waters.
Pelagic Sealing

In 1911 Canada had no treaty making powers, and after the signing of the treaty the enabling legislation was passed by the British parliament. It was not until 1913 that this parliament passed legislation with a view to controlling natives who might fit out boats on the Pacific coast or along Canadian shores for purposes of fishing on the high seas. Since 1911 we have been operating under the legislation I have indicated; but last year, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, a situation arose which, in my view, necessitated the revision of the then legislation. There was some room for difference of opinion as to whether or not we had the necessary machinery to punish those who violated the provisions of the treaty.
It mighlt be well for the committee to understand that through the treaty of 1911 Canada has relinquished any claim to property in the seals frequenting the waters. The United States claimed they owned a herd; Russia claimed they owned a herd, and Japan made a similar claim because, as was pointed out, the herds were found in the neighbourhood of islands within the territorial waters of those countries.
By virtue of our agreeing in 1911 not to interfere with the property of those countries with respect to seals, we are being allotted each year a certain number of skins, the valuable part of the seal. We receive a certain number of skins from the seals destroyed under the supervision of the governments of the United States, Russia and Japan. We receive those skins in return for helping those countries to protect the herds of seals by refusing rights to people from this country to fit out vessels on our shores and to go to sea hunting for seals, and for generally contributing towards the enforcement of the treaty.
The governments of the United States, Russia and Japan permit their natives to destroy or kill a certain number of seals each year, and under the provisions of the treaty we are granted fifteen per cent of the furs of seals killed by the United States, fifteen per cent from Japan, and ten per cent from Russia. Those skins are delivered each year at Victoria by the countries in question. The skins are sold at auction at St. Louis, Missouri, and London. From the sale of skins allotted to us we have derived SI,493,540.71 since the inception of the treaty.
The white people along the coast of British Columbia have not participated in the killing of seals, but under article 4 of the treaty the aborigines or Indians along the coast are allowed certain privileges. In 1936 the proceeds
[Mr. Michaud.}
from the sale of skins from animals caught by them amounted to SI,888. In 1937 their share, according to departmental statistics, amounted to 2,671 skins.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext: What happened to the proceeds of the sale of skins?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext:
It goes into the consolidated revenue fund. It is not administered by the department, and is not charged against departmental expenditures. My information is that since 1911 payment has been made into and made part of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
I find that the skins are sent either to London or to St. Louis, depending upon the state of the market. I am informed that these are the two great fur markets of the world. The furs are sold at auction and the proceeds are paid into the treasury of the dominion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext: Does that take place in regard to skins from Russia and Japan?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext: Yes; that is my information. I know that has happened in the last two years, and records of the department show it happened before that time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext: Do we take the skins or cash?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext: In the last few years we have taken the skins, but I am informed that prior to that we took cash. I am informed that for some years the skins have been delivered at either Victoria or Seattle. Russian and Japanese skins are delivered at Victoria, and the share contributed by the United States is delivered at Seattle.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext: Has Japan given her share in recent years? I think not.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext: I believe so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext: I think not.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext: I think so. We take the word of the governments of those countries, and I do not know of any investigation being made to ascertain whether or not we were getting exactly the proper number.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext: My impression is that in the last two or three years the Japanese have not paid their share. If I am wrong, I am ready to apologize, but the minister ought to know.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext:
I may be wrong, but I understood the difficulty was with Russia, that they had been late in making returns in one or two years. However, I am not positive about that. It may be that Japan delayed in

Pelagic Sealing
making her returns, but I doubt it. My information is that they have made returns regularly. However, I shall find out and give this information to my hon. friend as it appears on the records of the department before we finish discussing this bill in committee.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni has complained that this bill contains more clauses than the original act. This is necessary in order to administer the legislation. It was found advisable to provide in the bill for the necessary machinery to administer the act as it should be administered. The original act passed in 1913 implemented the provisions of an order in council passed by the British government. At that time it was thought that the fisheries legislation provided the necessary procedure and machinery to enforce the provisions of the act. This matter was looked into after the hon. member directed the attention of the department to the anomalies of which he complained. It was suggested that in order to remove all doubt the act should be recast and the necessary provisions included to cover all cases as they might arise.

speechtext: It states here that every regulation shall be published in the Canada Gazette. Were the regulations referred to by the minister published in the Gazette?

speechtext: I cannot say.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext: I have never seen them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext: It was before my time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext:
Is not this the situation? There has not been the least attempt made to put any penal clauses in the act. I think we might as well admit that and then go on. My contention is that there were never any regulations which were legal in the sense of having been gazetted. I think it will be found that the deputy minister, or an assistant deputy minister, wrote to the customs people and asked them if they saw any skins which they did not like the look of to seize them. I have seen those instructions. I did not think this matter would come up in this shape and I do not have them under my hand. I am very much of the opinion that they were not in the form of regulations; they were in the form of a letter from the deputy minister, or with the authority of the minister, to the customs people, asking them .to detain any skins which they had reason to believe had been obtained illegally. Those instructions were concentrated, so to speak, at Victoria.
Pelagic Sealing

Apparently it has now been discovered that those instructions did not have the force of law. Last July the deputy minister made an attempt to enforce them, but he found that he had not anything to enforce. The customs people seized some skins on his instructions, but the people who owned the skins asked for their authority. There was no authority, and this legislation is the outcome. I say that we should forget the past and deal with the future. What kind of regulation has the minister in mind with regard to inspection? These skins should be inspected by some one readily accessible to the Indians. The skins ought not to be sent to Vancouver or Victoria, as at present. They ought not to be inspected by customs officers who may not know whether they are seal or lion skins; they should be inspected by some officer of the department having knowledge of fishing, by somebody who knows something about it, and if possible always the same officer in the same district. It is a comparatively small district, and a couple of customs officers might do the work, but fisheries inspectors would be much better. They are capable men and maintain a continuity of policy, so to speak, and they would come to know by practical experience whether a skin was illegally shot. It is quite simple for anyone to break the law by coming along in a canoe and taking a 32 rifle and shooting, and the temptation would be to shoot the seal, and then poke a spear through the hole made by the shot. Now it is alleged they go and shoot them with shotguns. But I doubt that. The Indian is not a fool. He may be a lawbreaker. But every time you use buckshot it makes the skin less valuable; the Indian would be penalized when he sold it, and it would be obvious on a cursory inspection that the seal had been shot. I cannot believe the Indian would do that.
But these men say: Yes, here are these skins with shot-holes in them, and therefore the seals must have been shot. That is what the case turns on that is now before the exchequer court. There may be buckshot holes in them, but that does not prove that they were illegally shot. I was in the butchering business at one time, and I have killed cows that had a lot of small shot-holes in their skins because some indignant gardener had fired at them. It is a well known fact that the white fishermen who go out trolling for salmon get so mad pulling up their lines and finding nothing but heads on them that they take a shotgun and fire at a seal if they see one, not to kill it, but to scare it away, to

keep it clear of their lines. It is quite possible that some of these skins might have been shot in that way, and later on have been speared legitimately. Therefore I say this legislation should be administered by somebody who knows these things. It does not follow, because there is a buckshot hole in the skin, that therefore the poor Indian is responsible. I have seen hides of cattle with holes in them as big as your thumb due to an insect called a warble that makes a hole like a bullet hole. Is the minister going to arrange for some practical men, some persons easily accessible to the Indian, to do the inspecting, and will there be some method of marking the skins so that if an offence has been committed you can get back to the real sinner?
The exchequer court case is that of a storekeeper who bought the skins and paid cash for them to the Indian, and as you never can get cash back from an Indian, the storekeeper is now confronted with the loss of the skins. You cannot say whether the skins were shot illegally or not. The department should have said that in future the purchaser must be more careful, and the department then have legislation such as this passed. Is it the intention to proceed along these lines that I have been suggesting?

of this legislation is to remedy the situation which has just been described by my hon. friend and to obviate the difficulties which have arisen in the past year. The regulations which it is proposed to make under this legislation will meet the situation described by my hon. friend.

speechtext: I would like to renew the appeal I made a short time ago. Why not put the Indian on the same footing as the large vessel owner? It is against common sense-I do not know about law-for the reasons I have already given that it should be possible for a fisheries official, a man without any legal training whatsoever, to confiscate a boat, and then afterwards it may be discovered that the man was innocent of the crime for which the boat was seized and confiscated. If any person (other than an Indian or other aborigine in respect of the exercise of the privilege reserved by article 4 of the convention) uses any port within Canada for the purpose of equipping any vessel intended to be operated or used for any purpose whatsoever connected with the operations of pelagic sealing

And so forth. That would be persons who were operating a large vessel. It would be valuable property which we would not allow an ordinary officer to seize and forfeit to his majesty without process of law. But section 8 deals with the Indian who generally operates in a canoe.

In a canoe or other vessel. It is generally a small craft that the Indians use for this work because they know they are violating the law and they try to conceal their method of operation as much as possible. The value of the property is not such that we should place the offender in the position of
having	to defend	forfeiture	proceedings,
incurring a large amount of costs, and the same with respect to the department in prosecuting.
