speechtext:
I would not insist on the
case going to the exchequer court because that is an expensive proceeding, but it should go to any superior court such as the county court.	I wonder	where	our	CooperativeCommonwealth Federation	and	communisticfriends	are to-day.	They	would have just
heard a pronouncement that will ring throughout Canada, that if a large vessel is seized the case must go to the exchequer court, but if it is only a small vessel, worth only 81,000 or so, owned by an Indian, it can be confiscated on sight. That is a terrible position to put this parliament in. My protest is registered against that proceeding. What I have said cannot be gainsaid.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION
speechtext:
I agree with the hon.
member who has just spoken. This is a serious matter to an Indian or one operating a small vessel. The vessel is likely to be of some value, in fact a very great value to the Indian; it will be one that can go to sea and will probably be equipped with a gas engine; probably it will represent almost the entire possessions of the Indian. May I suggest to the minister-and I should like the Minister of Justice to listen to this suggestion-that at the end of clause 8, instead of saying-
. . . may be seized by any officer authorized under the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act to board and search, and shall be forfeited to His Majesty.
-words should be used somewhat to this effect:
. . . shall be held pending the decision of a court in the matter.
The Minister of Justice could easily frame something of this kind. The idea is to give the seizing officer only the right to hold the vessel in order to hold the man. I quite understand that if an Indian, having been arrested for this offence, were allowed to go with his boat, it might be difficult to find him again, but the vessel could be held pending the determination of his guilt. It will be noted that in section 11 penalties are provided for violations of the act, so that there is no need to insert in this clause an added penalty against the Indian by the seizure of his vessel. I agree with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni that it is more serious to an Indian to lose his vessel than it would be to a group of individuals in the form of a company who have equipped a
Pelagic Sealing

vessel for such a purpose. I know how this all arises. In days gone by-and I remember it very well, thirty-five or forty years ago- it was one of the glorious practices of seafaring folk on the Pacific coast to equip vessels, as dozens of them did in Victoria and some at Vancouver and other places, and go out poaching and killing seals. It was a real thrill to the men who operated those vessels. I knew some of them well. One whom I knew personally very well indeed was the "Sea Wolf," and one could not help but admire the spectacular type of individual he was. but he was utterly unscrupulous so far as poaching seals was concerned. A law that provides against the equipping of vessel? under such circumstances is quite right; but where an Indian goes out and is tempted to kill a fewr seals, although I am not condoning the offence, to take from him his whole livelihood on the say-so of an officer authorized under the Customs or Fisheries Protection Act is giving to that individual a power and a right w'hich I do not think should be given to any individual. So I suggest to the minister that the words as printed be struck out and that there be substituted the power to detain or hold the vessel.

Knowing as they do that they cannot build a bridge beyond the medial line of the river, the only thing left to do is to create a real estate boom. Why? Because when this matter was considered on another occasion I recall that it was pointed out very clearly-my hon. friend the surveyor (Mr. Fafard) smiles-that under the old International there had grown up certain well-defined rights. People had built homes; the traffic had been diverted in a certain way. But now, before we have the right to build a bridge at all, with that prohibition against our doing anything about it, we are going to authorize them to buy all the real estate they want and to place their plans before the governor in council, and notwithstanding the prohibition, " to do all things authorized by this act." What does that mean? If that is not a plain contradiction in terms, I cannot understand what a contradiction is. On the one hand you have the condition that nothing shall be done until the United States has granted authority, and on the other side what? The permission to do all things authorized by this act. Surely, Mr. Chairman, we have not reached that stage.
It is all right to say that you must read the two together, and I tried to do that. When you read them together as a whole, what have you? You cannot do anything until the act of the United States authority permits you to land the bridge over there. That is No. 1. But before that is done-and that permission has already been refused- they can in the meantime acquire the lands, submit plans to the governor in council, and do all things authorized by this act. That only proves one thing, and that is that the authority
to build the bridge is improperly given. It must be to build a bridge to the centre of the stream, and to that point only, because obviously the governor in council cannot be given approval to what has not any substance in law. What plans are they going to approve? They cannot approve plans for constructing beyond the middle of the stream. How could they? In the meantime the only plans they could submit would be plans to the centre of the stream, because otherwise they would be dealing with plans of the United States of America, over which it is admitted they now have no power.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As this is the first day that we are going into committee on the fisheries estimates I should like to make a statement dealing with some points in connection with that industry. Possibly some of them are only local; others are certainly provincial; some of them are national and one matter at least might fairly be called international. I thought perhaps it would be fairer to the minister and the department to make my statement at this time so that he might have an opportunity of looking up these various matters before they come up on the detailed estimates in committee of supply.
The first matter I want to present, and about which I desire to register a mild protest, is the custom that has grown up, not only under this minister but under previous ministers, of allowing a subordinate officer in British Columbia to issue a statement to the press containing what is called a review of the situation as regards the fisheries of British Columbia, without first submitting that review to the head office of the department. The relations between head office and the office at Vancouver are not my business, if that is the way they prefer to do things-to have a man out there tell them not only what they should do, but what they are going to do. But I do protest, when it becomes a source of trouble to fishermen, and to people who represent fishermen. Unfortunately it sometimes becomes not a review, but a preview, and announcements are made as to what the policy of the government is going to be. Sometimes the government's policy is not in accord with the announcement that is made, and this causes a lot of trouble.
Recently an extensive review was published. The review was a long one, because the compressed report in the papers took up nearly a column of print. It leaves the impression, as evidenced by the big headlines, that the department have in hand some scheme or method by which fishermen can obtain loans in order to enable them to buy better and bigger boats. That is a very nice idea, indeed; I am all for it. I have advocated it for years. In fact, I believe the minister himself two years ago introduced some scheme of the kind. But British Columbia did not accept the offer he made. Now

British Columbia Fisheries
the department says it has no such scheme before it. I have letters from fishermen asking how they are going to get in under this new scheme which is to be evolved. This makes trouble. It may be alleged, perhaps correctly, that the official did not definitely use that language; but that is the impression he conveyed to the press, and the press indicated it by printing, in big headlines, "B.C. Fishermen May Get Money to Build Traps."
The fisherman does not discriminate between the use of the word "may" and the use of the expression "is going to." They expect that that is going to be carried out. I submit a lot of trouble would have been saved if the official in question had not issued these reviews, or previews, without first submitting them to the department at Ottawa. I wonder if the minister-or any minister- would allow a deputy, or any subordinate official here, to announce what the policy of a department was going to be? That is what happened in this case and, as I have said, it makes trouble.
May I point out that with the idea of getting a proper conception of the alleged proposals I asked for a copy of the review- once on the fourth, twenty-two days ago, and again on the eleventh. But I have not yet had them given to me. Either the deputy in the west has not seen fit to forward them, or the minister here has not seen fit to furnish me with a copy. In any event, I think the principle is an unhappy one, and should be abandoned. It is not only to-day that this trouble has occurred; it has also occurred in the past.
The next matter I should like to deal with is a local one-and I am sorry to bore the house with local matters. I assure hon. members that it is only after long correspondence and after permitting myself to be stalled for several years in the hope that the very obvious facts-the unalterable and logical facts-would bring the government to take action in the matter. Apparently that has not been done, and I am forced to bring the matter to the court of last resort. It reveals a record of stupidity and neglect, and a refusal to face obvious and inescapable facts, and to deal with existing conditions.
The matter is linked with Comox lake, a lake five miles from Courtenay. Into that lake streams and creeks run from higher ground, and provide an ideal spawning place. Then, out of Comox lake runs the Puntledge river, to the sea, some five or six miles lower down. Some twenty-five years ago a colliery company wishing to establish a source of power built a dam on the Puntledge river. That was in 1913. The law is that the owners of dams must, on the request of the Department of Fisheries, put in suitable fish ladders.
So far as I can ascertain, and so far as the records show, the department made no attempt to do that, until individuals and boards of trade alarmed by the drop in the amount of fish running in that direction, stirred them up. It took a couple of years before any action could be obtained. But in 1920 the department did take some action. They obtained a report from one of their officials, a man who had been twenty years in the service and who had intimate local knowledge, a man whose reputation stands high. He has since left the service. This is what he said:
I am not in a position to state whether salmon got into the lake in any quantities before the impounding dam was built, but it is a fact that now they do try to get into it and are prevented from reaching the lake owing to the present structure of the dam. I have been up the lake on several occasions and have carefully inspected the nature of the bottom of it anti i am convinced that no better spawning ground could be found anywhere. . . [DOT] In my opinion as fishery officer I have no hesitation in saying that I most certainly consider that a suitable fish ladder should he erected in the impounding dam.
Not satisfied with that, the department consulted a real expert in such matters, an expert in the culture of fish and the operation of hatcheries. He was a very able man, and now occupies a very responsible position, doing the same kind of work for the provincial government. He made this statement, which is even stronger:
I can state, without hesitation, that the Cruiksliank river wffiich enters the lake from the north, and Beadnell creek entering the head of the lake, offers spawning grounds unsurpassed in quality and extent, by any I have seen in other parts of the province.
British Columbia abounds in rivers in which there are salmon and fish of all kinds. When experts say that Comox lake and its tributary creeks provide the best spawning grounds to be found anywhere in the province, they are saying something worthy of attention. He described the fish attempting to pass up the dam as being variously described as "crowds", "lots" and "hundreds". He ended up by saying that he considered the number of fish attempting to enter the lake fully justified the expenditure of installing an efficient fishway. People might believe that any body of water would do for salmon spawning, but that is not so. Special conditions are required. There must be a special kind of bottom soil, or gravel. And, for most classes of fish there must be, as in Comox lake, creeks entering the lake. The fish go up the river, into the lake. Then they go into the creeks to spawn.
British Columbia Fisheries

Then they go down, after spawning, and stay a year in the fresh water of the lake, following which they go out to sea again, to fulfil their destiny. That is true of the two most important and valuable salmon, the sockeye and the cohoe. So that when both these men specializing in the culture of fish have spoken in the manner indicated, surely it is urgent and important that we take steps to develop such wonderful spawning grounds. Both the sockeye and the cohoe, as I have indicated, go into the creeks above Comox lake. No sockeye are in there at the present time. There was an attempt made to introduce them, but apparently it failed. But it can be done, because it has been done in other places, and the conditions are ideal.
But the cohoes were there, and they are not there to-day. The sockeye is the most valuable commercial fish; but the cohoe, while commercially valuable, has a much greater value in its opportunity for development as a sporting fish. It has been discovered only in recent years that they will take a fly and, as they make a tremendous fight, they become valuable as a sporting fish. All the world knows, however, about the big spring salmon taken in that neighbourhood. They come from all over the world as the club records show. The cohoe sport will not be competitive with that, but will be supplementary to it, and will add tremendously in increasing sporting facilities for the tourist trade. It is estimated that every tourist who comes from afar to take one of these large springs will leave anywhere from a hundred to five hundred dollars in the province for each fish he takes.
Incidentally the cohoe is a valuable fish to the working fisherman. All a man needs is a rowboat to go out to make a start. This type of fishing does not require any nets; they do it by what is called trolling. It offers an opportunity to the working fisherman to get a living with the least possible expenditure.
An agitation was stirred up by the public and by the boards of trade, and the officials of the department told the company that they would have to put in a ladder, which they did in 1922. The first blunder was in not making the company do it a number of years before, and the second blunder was in allowing the installation of this type of ladder in the place where it was installed. The proper place to have put it was at the end of the dam in the solid rock where it would have been permanent and effective. It should have consisted of a series of pools about two and a half or three feet above each other. The

fish could jump from one to the other, almost like children jumping up a stairway. This type of ladder has been a tremendous success in a similar river near Alberni where tourists come from all over just to watch the fish going up.
Because it would be cheaper for the company, they were permitted to install what is known as the Hocken type of fish ladder. This ladder consists of an opening eighteen inches deep and a certain number of feet wide in the bottom of the dam. This ladder worked for a while in a sort of way as some fish got up after it wias put in. But it was workable only under ideal and unusual conditions; that is, when the water on one side of the dam balanced to some extent the water on the lower side. But when there was any large quantity of water; when there was high water in the river, it was impossible for the fish to get up. In order to do so they would have had to dive down and go through this hole through which there was a rush of water. It was like asking a minnow to go up a fireman's hose against a pressure of sixty pounds to the square inch. The fish simply could not go up unless the water was fairly well balanced. The error was made in allowing this type of ladder, but it was done because it would be cheaper for the company. The company has rebuilt the ladder twice. The ladder has been constructed three times and it has washed out again, so it was not any economy for the company. At no time was it effective, and for the last three years, certainly for the last two years and a half, it has been a total failure. Later on the company wanted more power and they raised the head of the dam some three or four feet.
The ladder was washed out in 1927 and was replaced that year by the company. The same type of ladder was put in on the advice of the officials. Then it was washed out again in 1934 and replaced in 1935, and it was washed out again last December. When it was rebuilt in 1935, it was moved somewhat to meet the changed condition of higher water, but it was not placed at the end of the dam as it should have been. The result was worse than it was before. I think I can safely say that there have been no fish go up since. There is a record of one trout that was believed to have been found above the dam. The company is not to blame as they put in what they were ordered to put in. They constructed the ladder three times at their own expense, and I understand they are now saying to the department that they have done their part; that they have done what they were told to

British Columbia Fisheries
do, and that if the department cannot devise a ladder which will be effective and permanent, they had better do it themselves.
I asked a question as to what the cost of this ladder had been and I received a reply that that information was not available as the fish ladder was built and installed by the owner of the dam. That is quite correct, but I have in my hand a letter from one official to another in which the cost of the first ladder is given and an estimate of the second ladder is made. This is not very important, but it illustrates how determined the department is not to give information that they do not want to give. Perhaps I could now suggest that the department is to blame in the matter, but I am not altogether prepared to do that. It is easy to be wise after the event, and possibly if I had been in their position I would have made the same error, but I certainly would not have assumed the attitude that they assumed subsequently. I do blame the department for refusing to recognize results and facts.
They spent two or three years trying to prove that I was wrong, trying to prove that people who had lived there all their lives did not know what they were talking about. The department contended that fish were going up when in fact they were not. Some years ago I made a sporting offer. I said: Let us forget whose fault it is, let us unite to try to get the situation remedied. But the officials of the department are like the Medes and Persians, perhaps far more so; if they once say a thing is so, then it cannot possibly be proved to be wrong. They were so determined not to admit the thing was a failure that they built a trap above the dam to catch the fish that they were sure were going through, but they did not get even a sucker. They now admit that the thing is a failure and that the cohoe run has been killed. I have under my hand six letters from various officials, all of which state in more or less precise language that that is so. They admit the run is killed; they admit the ladder is no use, and still they do nothing.
Then, in order to put themselves right, they turn around and say: Well, after all, the cohoe did not go up into the lake; they spawned in the river. Tell that to any fisherman and he will laugh at you. They may spawn in the river below the dam under certain circumstances, but they are not successful. How can they be when there is a record a couple of years ago that that area below the dam was dry for three weeks? They want to go up, not only into the lake but into the' streams above the lake. Then they said: Well, perhaps .after all the fish never did go into the lake,
even before the dam was built. If that is so, what can be said about the report of their own officials? What is to be said about the fact that they compelled this company three times to build the ladder? What about the expert who said that there were lots of fish going up? I think I might quote from one letter which is typical and illustrative of what the officials say. This reads:
Indeed, I have gone back on the original records in the department about the matter, and I find that as long ago as 1898 the then commissioner of fisheries in dealing with natural obstructions in a lower portion of the river stated that "at present the river is of small importance as a salmon river."
Of course it was of small importance as a salmon river forty years ago. Those were the days when the salmon were so thick in the Fraser and Skeena rivers and their tributaries that the cannery men put a quota on the fishermen. They would take only 200 fish a night from each boat. After that they had to throw them overboard or stay in. Of course this river was of no importance as a salmon river forty years ago because the salmon could be caught more easily and in greater numbers in other rivers. That is a very poor argument to use to support the contention that they should abandon the river now when every river and stream is important.
As I have said, this ladder was washed away last December. I asked what steps had been taken towards replacing it, and I was told that the need for requiring replacement was under consideration. It has been under consideration for three years and we are not any further ahead than we were then. We have reports from two officials stating specifically that conditions as they are now could not be improved. If you are willing to abandon this spawning ground which has been stated by experts to be the best or at least as good as any in British Columbia; if you are willing to abandon this run of cohoe salmon which is so valuable for sporting purposes and to the working fisherman, then I suppose it is all right if you are prepared to accept that situation.
When the hatchery was abandoned some years ago, it was mentioned in this house that we should devote more and more time to natural propagation, to the encouragement of runs by natural means. This is the case in point and this is just exactly what we are not doing. I have no use for faultfinders who do not suggest a remedy. I have indicated what is wrong and here is what I think is needed. We need a fish ladder like the one they built some years ago on the Stamp river near Alberni. It was entirely successful. It has renewed the run of sockeye salmon, which is
British Columbia Fisheries

a very valuable asset, furnishing employment for 200 men, and of advantage from a tourist point of view as well. Put the ladder in at the right place, around the end of the dam, and it will be permanent and therefore effective. I have no brief for the colliery company. They have as little use'for me as I for them; but fair is fair, and if anything further is to be done it should be done at the expense of the government. The colliery company were told to put the ladder in the wrong place, and it was of the non-effective type. So much for that item.
Next I want to protest against the method of handling herrings in British Columbia. I am referring now to the reducing of herrings. To those not familiar with it I may say that reducing herrings is a method of squeezing the oil out of them, and by some process of applying acid they reduce the residue into what is called fish meal, which is largely used as fertilizer and to some extent for stock feed. I maintain that that is a waste of a valuable food fish. There is an ample market, if it was pushed, for putting up herrings in the shape of canned and smoked herrings, canned in oil, kippers, and so on. In that way we would give the largest amount of labour and get the most money value out of a given quantity of fish; but by reducing them we get the very least amount of labour, and it is the least profitable, and requires an enormous catch to make it profitable to operate. The result is that it depletes the herring spawning grounds.
There is an important industry there of reducing pilchards, which is very much more profitable for several reasons. They are much more full of oil, containing double the amount found in herrings sometimes, and that makes it more profitable. Pilchards do not spawn in our water, so we cannot take too many of them, so to speak. Pilchards are to a large extent not cannable, because they are so oily, and there is not a good demand for them.
The department will say; I have heard them say, that we cannot and do not deplete the run of the herring on the spawning grounds because it would be trying to dip out the ocean, so to speak, and you cannot do that. That is true in a way, but herrings do not spawn in the ocean like pilchards, but spawn in narrow, confined waters, in bays and inlets. I have seen seine boats like a procession of motor cars, one waiting until the other one pulled out of the only good place in the bay, and there would be a continual succession until the bay was cleaned out. You do not eliminate herrings. You cannot catch them all, but you can harass them until they go

away. I can name harbours-Nanaimo is one-where the herring were taken almost inside the town itself, almost at the door of the hotel. They treated them like that and the herring went away and did not come back for fifteen or twenty years. That is what herring will do if you harass them enough. It is not that you take all the herrings, but that they abandon the spawning ground.
There was a large run of herring last year, the department will say, due to taking in large new areas, and incidentally because of the incidence of the gulf stream, which in certain years comes nearer our shores and brings more marine growth, which the fish follow. The experts say that the size of the fish taken indicates that they are being depleted.
I have not yet mentioned the principal thing about the herrings. The principal thing is that they are feed for salmon, and are sought for by the spring salmon, as they are called. I have a quotation here from a fisherman. It is headed in big type "No herring, no salmon," and reads:
Prohibit the reduction of herring and good times will return to the salmon trollers. This is the considered advice of Pete Larsen.
He is a fisherman from Norway, well known on our coast.
According to Pete, the trollers have not even made expenses in the past month and lie blames it on the wholesale destruction of herring which provide the salmon's natural food. ^
"No herring, no salmon!" is Mr. Larsens firm conviction.
Even if they do not clean out the herrings, they break up the schools and then the salmon do not follow them so readily. I suggest that we should follow the system adopted in Norway. I have some data in connection with that. I do not think Norway reduces herrings at all. If it does, it is only from offal. Most of their herring go into canning, and they can them in sixteen different ways. I shall not mention them all, but they have smoked herring, unsmoked, herrings canned in oil, in tomatoes, and so on. They make the very best use of their herring in that way, and get the most money from them. Norway, with a population of sixty per cent less than the maritime provinces of Canada, including British Columbia, in that sense, in 1935 and 1936, the last two years for which records were available, exported 74,000 tons of canned herring, not raw herring, while we in Canada with all that much greater population exported exactly 1,428 tons-74,000 tons as against 1,400 tons, or about 6,000 per cent more. And Norway received $228 per ton for its herrings, while we received 8145 for

British Columbia Fisheries
ours-quite a difference. They get the most out of their herrings by putting them up in oil, in tomatoes, and so on. I suggest that we should develop our herring industry along the line of Norway's system. But the difference as between 8228 and $145 per ton is only minor compared with the difference between canning them and reducing them, and that is what I want to go into.
In British Columbia in 1937 we used approximately 84.000 tons of fresh herring for reduction purposes. That is a lot of fish to be converted into fertilizer meal and oil. We got a price that netted us for our fresh fish S9.50 a ton, of which the seagoing fishermen who caught them would get $2.25 a ton, split seven ways, and an extra share for the boat; so each fisherman actually got only one-eighth of S2.25 per ton for every ton he helped to catch; sometimes it would be $2.50.
I ask, Is it good policy to allow the reduction of herrings under those circumstances, there being very little profit to the producer owing to the low oil content; also it depletes the spawning grounds and destroys the food of the salmon, particularly that of the springs. A fisherman can go out at night or in the morning and troll for springs, and if he catches only one large spring he will get more for that one fish than if he went out in a herring seine boat and participated in a catch of five or six tons of fresh herring. I think we should feature Norway's way of doing it, and develop our industry along those lines. It uses less fish, and does not add to the output of pilchard oil and meal, because the market for that is somewhat restricted; the pilchard industry can take care of it in any event, and if you overload the market the price goes down. You would get $225 a ton as against $9.50 a ton-a far bigger return. Therefore I say we should stop reducing herrings. I think that is the logical and reasonable thing to do.
The next item on the list is the question of fish traps. We heard a lot about it last year in the committee, and I do not propose to take up the time of the house with it now. But I have the report in my hand, and it says:
That no more trap licences be granted in British Columbia waters except in the so called Soolce area, and concerning which we are unable to come to a decision as to whether they should be continued or not, without the opportunity of securing further information.
I might also say that that report recommended that the licence for each trap should be raised from $50 to $500, a little increase of a thousand per cent, the difference between $350 for the lot, and $3,500

which, most significantly, met no objection from the two
companies who owned and operated these traps. It also suggested that we should get certain data as to what was caught in the traps.
Some weeks ago I presented to this house a petition with approximately ten thousand names on it, petitioning against the further use of traps in British Columbia. I may say that it was no political device. Nobody was paid to go around and collect the signatures. It was a spontaneous movement. The total expense at least as far as I was concerned was three or four dollars for printing the petition, because I thought it would look better if we had it printed. It met with a very large and very quick response. In the light of the petition I thought that possibly the minister, the department or the government, whoever is responsible, would either stop the traps this year or send the matter to the committee to consider the data obtained. I have before me some of this data. I shall not go fully into it, but it is quite illuminating. They caught three quarters of a million fish, and one might almost say they caught everything, from whales to shrimps. That would be an exaggeration, but they caught one whale, one porpoise, a number of wolf fish, barracuda, sharks, sea lions, hake, herrings, ratfish, sturgeon, and of course, all kinds of salmon. It must have been a comprehensive operation when it took everything from a whale down to a herring. The minister, I regret to say, voicing the views of the department, refused either to stop the traps or to refer the matter again to the committee; their motto was that of the French war heroes, " They shall not pass"; he would not even discuss the matter. So far as my knowledge goes, that brings the matter to an impasse; it is impossible to go any further at the present time. I can only say that it must wait until the next general election, which I anticipate will take place this fall.

The nest item is one which comes home, or should come home, to every man and woman in Canada. It is the most vital thing in British Columbia fisheries; upon it depends the whole existence of the salmon, cod and halibut fisheries. It is not a question of cutting down overfishing; it is elimination, wiping them out. I allude to the destruction caused by the "Japs," if I may use that word, by intensive and unrestrictive fishing outside the three mile limit. Unfortunately, as far as we know, they are within their legal rights; they are outside territorial waters, where it is open to the whole world to fish. It was suggested that a Norwegian boat was coming around, and that a British boat intended to fish for halibut. Either representations were made or something else happened; for some reason or another they did not come.
But the greatest danger in any event would be from the Japanese, because they are best suited owing to their nearness, their experience, and the ruthless methods which they have never hesitated to employ. Their idea of fishing is to take every fish as long as you can see one, and then go somewhere else. They did that with their own fishing grounds off their own coast. Then, having by some means obtained fishing from the Russians, they proceeded to do the same thing there, and now they have come to Alaska and are carrying on in the same way. Later, British Columbia will be the victim. I might explain how it is done. They bring a great big mother ship across the ocean, able to carry launches like the schooners on the Atlantic carry dories; they anchor outsde the three mile limit, where the salmon runs are, and they fish intensively and relentlessly and with no regard to time, season or conservation. They put the fish on board, process them, can them, freeze them or whatever is required in the way of preparation, and then go home with, I was going to say, their bloody spoils, but their fishy spoils would be more correct. The United States government is seriously alarmed. They obtain an income of seventy million dollars from their salmon in Alaska, and they see it seriously imperilled. This is no wild idea of visionary men looking into the future; it is going on to-day; it has been going on for the last couple of years.
In an article published in Japan not long ago, it was stated:
The Behring sea has become an arm of Tokyo bay.

That must be nice reading for the Americans. A fleet of one hundred and one Japanese vessels this summer was strung along the coast of Bristol bay, Alaska, for two hundred miles. Think of it! Two hundred miles! Ostensibly they were after crabs. Yes, they said they were only prospecting for crabs. Their intentions were as innocent as regards salmon and halibut as their intentions as regards a certain nation alongside them are or were supposed to be. Unfortunately there are resources of modern science; the fishing people sent out aeroplanes from Alaska; they took photographs of twenty thousand fish on the decks of this mother ship; they went so close that they could even discern, not the signs of the times but the names stamped on the cases of packed salmon; they swooped down within a hundred feet. There is not a question but that that is going on. Now, as I understand, having their attention occupied elsewhere, they have agreed with the United States not to send any more ships over for the present, for the next year. They said that last year. I suppose that is one of those famous or infamous gentleman's agreements which are used only so long as it is profitable to adhere to them. One United States congressman has been asked to introduce a bill in congress declaring that any fish spawned in Alaskan waters belong to the American people, the same as we might say that any fish spawned in the Fraser river belong to us. It is rather a far-fetched thing, and it would not apply as regards halibut, for they do not spawn in our waters. The United States might perhaps establish a claim to shut off the Bering sea as a clausum mare, on the ground that the coast line is from headland to headland; but considering the enormous size of the Bering sea, which is not a bay but a sea, I am doubtful whether such a claim could be upheld.
We made a wonderful treaty three years ago with the United States. Under it the halibut fisheries have been built up; the catch is much greater and much more assured of permanence; but this is just going to be wiped out because the Japanese or any other foreigners can anchor off our banks

the fish are to be found in certain defined areas-and clean them up. Now there must be some way of stopping that. If it is not stopped, all our fishing goes; all our regulations, and the army of officials we maintain, our close seasons and restrictions all go by the board. If we are going to lose the fish anyhow, we might as well clean them out ourselves. There must be some means, diplomacy perhaps, of having a surcease in this matter. Speaking offhand and out of

British Columbia Fisheries
my own ignorance, I suggest this: The biggest market the Japanese fishermen have for canned salmon is in the United States and Great Britain. If the United States and Great Britain would say: If you are not going to cease this cutthroat policy, so ruinous alike to yourselves and us, we will not let a tin of your canned salmon into either the United States or Great Britain. That would bring them to time.
This is a most important matter, a matter for diplomacy rather than departmental action. Our ambassador to Japan might well enter into negotiations concerning it, instead of making himself a willing conduit for the dissemination in Canada of Japanese propaganda against, to us, a friendly nation. He would be much better employed in doing that. If he has been doing anything of that kind let him announce it; it would make him a lot more popular in British Columbia, where his stock is anything but high at the present time. If there have been negotiations going on, let us know the result. Anything would be welcome provided it was not in the form of a gentlemen's agreement. I say with all respect to the minister that he has rather withdrawn himself behind a wall of silence for the last three years; let him come out from behind that wall and use the ability which we believe he possesses to deal with these matters. Let us know the best and the worst. It is well to know the worst, because we have to know it sooner or later. Let him tell us what has been attempted in these matters and what his future policy is, and we shall have confidence in him, and I am sure many hon. members, including myself, would be very glad to give him every possible support.
Just two other small matters. One is that the dominion has lately handed over to British Columbia the control of non-tidal waters as regards fishing. It is not clear whether they have handed over all the non-tidal fish or only the non-tidal sport fish; in that regard the order in council contradicts the Fisheries department letters. There is also difficulty by reason of there being such a divergence of fact in the matter. For instance, there are tidal sport fish and there are non-tidal commercial fish; so again the question arises, If the dominion is going to say, "We control the tidal fish and the province the non-tidal," where is the line to be drawn? I believe another difficulty has arisen in Quebec; there I do not think the term used is non-tidal so much; I think it is the waters above the navigable portions of the St. LawTence. However, there again is opportunity for dispute and doubt as to where the dividing line is.
I am told that according to the British North America Act the province could demand control of its non-tidal fish. Possibly so, but surely the British North America Act is not responsible for the anomalous situation which I am now going to describe. It seems that the dominion still has control of the regulations, because apparently under the British North America Act we control the regulation and catch of fish, while the province can claim the right in the fish in non-tidal waters. To suit the province apparently, the department, I think rather weakly, agreed to pass whatever regulations the province asked them to do. Now there is going to be trouble about that, and very soon. Some day the province is going to ask for some foolish, ill-advised regulation. Suppose they took it into their head to put poison in a lake in order to get rid of some predatory fish, and in doing so poisoned the run of valuable fish; or suppose someone ate some of those poisoned fish. Who would be responsible? We would. We have the responsibility under the British North America Act; we cannot evade our responsibility. The department must in some way have sensed that danger, because I see in a recent Gazette, in giving out some regulations in connection with the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, they say it is done at the request of the department of agriculture of the provincial government. They are going to try to get out of their responsibility by saying, Bill Jones in Alberta or Tom Smith in Saskatchewan asked us to do it, and therefore we are not responsible. I think the lawyer members of the house will say that we cannot divest ourselves of our responsibility, and if anything wrong is done we would be responsible. I think the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Labour will agree that they have had sad experience of the inadvisability of the dominion government handing over either its authority to act or its cash for any province to use or spend.
Suppose, for instance-a more likely thing, and I have such a case in my mind-the province took a certain lake in its efforts for the encouragement of sport fishing. I could name a place where it might well happen. Suppose the dominion government have gone to great expense putting in a fish ladder and large quantities of fish fry to facilitate the run of sockeye salmon and have developed them in that lake, and they are proving valuable, a couple of hundred fishermen getting a livelihood from them. But suppose the province says, We are not concerned about your commercial fishing; all we are concerned with is sport fishing, and we are going to put sporting trout into this lake, which will live

British Columbia Fisheries

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Fisheries) :
maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for
Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) did not give me any previous intimation that he was going to take up these matters at this junction, so I am sure the house will not expect me to reply to everything he said or to give all the details in regard to the several matters which were mentioned by the hon. member. However, he is to be congratulated upon his noble effort and his appeal to the minister and the department for a statement of policy with the hope that something may be done to remedy the conditions of which he is complaining.
If we consider soberly the questions raised by the hon. member we must admit that they are in the main matters of detail, over which there have been differences of opinion in British Columbia and throughout Canada for a great many years, matters which it seems impossible to adjust in such a way as to satisfy all concerned. My hon. friend began by complaining of officials of departments who take upon themselves the responsibility of issuing statements which might be interpreted in some quarters as explaining or laying down the policies of the department or the government. Of course, in the Department of Fisheries, as in every other department of the government, we have human beings as officials, and they are liable to err and make mistakes. In this instance I find that it has been the policy of heads of branches in the areas in which they are stationed, particularly in the east and west, occasionally to make reports^ of what has been going on, covering their activities during the period of a year.

British Columbia Fisheries
The other day the hon. member brought to my attention a matter in regard to the annual review made some time ago by the supervisor of fisheries for British Columbia. I have looked into this matter. I asked for the report which was made, as I informed the hon. member, without being first submitted to the department. I find that it was a very general statement of facts, with the possible exception of one matter upon which a wrong interpretation was placed by some of the newspapers in British Columbia. The matter will be further explained when the exact words used by the official come before me and have been studied. Judging from the newspaper reports, however, I think some of the newspapers, as well as the hon. member, jumped to conclusions which were not warranted by the facts as reported in the press at the time. I may say at this point that these statements are not generally submitted to the minister before they are given out, because they are supposed to be statements of facts. If sometimes the imagination of the officials carries them away and they become too enthusiastic over their work, I suppose they will have to be disciplined or reminded that in future they should refrain from attempting to commit the department or the government to any policy.
Another matter of which the hon. member complained is the old question of the Punt-ledge river fish ladder. I find that this has been under consideration in the department ever since 1920. It appears that in 1913 Canadian Collieries Limited built a dam on the Puntledge river to develop water power and generate electricity to serve the people in that vicinity. It may be stated that from the information before me the dam is not at the mouth of the river but is some distance from Comox lake, which would be a suitable ground for spawning purposes. My information is to the effect that around 1917 some people thought a fishway should be built in that dam in order to facilitate the entrance of the fish to Comox lake. Since 1920 three attempts have been made to construct suitable fish ladders, not always at the same location; but unfortunately they did not hold; they were washed out, and at the present time there is no fishway in that dam. So far as I can judge from the records of the department, since 1920 every official charged with the administration of the regulations in that part of the country has tried to meet the situation as best he could. Many opinions have been offered by officials and by independent persons, but I believe the situation is very well expressed in the reports of the 51952-146J
district supervisor of fisheries and the chief supervisor of fisheries for British Columbia. Those reports have been made after many years of observation and study.
It is represented to the department by our engineers and officials who, we believe, are competent in such matters, that to. build a fishway at the place where it is suggested it should be built, namely on the left side of the dam, would certainly jeopardize the efficiency of the dam. If the fishway were cut through the rock at the side of the dam, there is no assurance that the salmon would use it, or that it would assist in any way to increase the run. Such a fishway would necessitate blasting pools in the rock on the left side of the stream, which would undoubtedly weaken the structure of the dam.
The towns of Cumberland and Courtenay, with populations of 2,371 and 1,219 respectively, as well as the towns of Comox and Royston, and the territory wtihin a radius of thirty-five miles, are dependent upon this source for power and light. It seems that there is not much evidence to show that above the power dam, to Comox lake, these waters have been frequented by large numbers of salmon. It is represented, and has been ascertained by officials of the department, that the different varieties of salmon frequenting these waters are being well maintained, and that there is sufficient room in the Puntledge river below Comox lake for the spawning of all salmon coming to the stream in recent years. In the opinion of the Courtenay-Comox boards of trade, and the affiliated fish and game association of Vancouver island, Comox lake is more valuable from the standpoint of sport fish than for salmon, and the latter association have asked that salmon be not introduced into Comox lake.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When did the board of trade recommend that?

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not sure exactly of the date, but I can find out the exact date that the recommendation was made.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: While the minister is looking for it, he might look for one dated last year, in which they recommended that the ladder should be put in, and the run of cohoes protected.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have a copy of it.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It goes to show that this is a difficult proposition, and that there is room for a wide difference of opinion. According to the hon. member, even the same people
British Columbia Fisheries

change their minds about the efficiency of building a ladder along the lines recommended by some people. Some think the plan would not be feasible and would jeopardize the efficiency of power development at that place.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Can the minister say how high the dam is?

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think I have the information here. This matter has been considered by various officials, and by my predecessors, since 1920, and we have all tried to give our best attention to the problem. It is our conclusion that it is not worth while to incur the necessary expenditures, and to jeopardize the good water power, in order to increase the spawning facilities in Comox lake, particularly when we feel that every facility is offered below the lake and below the dam, from the mouth of the river.
However, we are still looking into the matter and we hope some day to find a solution which will meet with the approval of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and of the board of trade.
Another matter which has been brought up has been the criticism of the method of handling herring in British Columbia. I admit that it. is a fish which is hard to handle in that province. We are told it would be much more profitable to can and smoke the herring rather than reduce it to fish meal. Well, that is another matter in connection with which there is room for great differences of opinion. I am not an expert in the matter, and I would not give my own opinion; but I find that for the last fifty years people from British Columbia, in this house and out of it, have given opinions, and have widely differed in their suggestions. But it seems to me that if it was so much more profitable to can or to smoke the herring rather than reduce it, there would be a sufficient number of intelligent people in British Columbia to go into that business. They could, or should, see the advantages of changing the method of handling the herring catch.
I am informed that about ten years ago the same proposition was advocated, and that some people tried canning rather than reducing the herring. It was found most unsatisfactory and unprofitable. However, I hope the hon. member will be able to convince people in the fishing industry to change their methods of handling that kind of fish, and if he is successful I can assure him that, so far as I am concerned, there will be no obstacles raised by the department.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Before the minister leaves that, would he permit me to speak on a question

of privilege? I have in my hand the communication to which I referred. The resolution passed by the Courtenay board of trade, after setting out various whereases, contains the following:
Therefore be it resolved, that the Minister of Fisheries be requested to see that an efficient fish ladder be installed at the Bevan dam.
That is dated January 12, 1937.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Has my hon. friend the other letter in which the other alternative was advocated?

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What date?

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not the date.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No. Has the minister the
letter?

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not here, but I shall
bring before the house the information on record in the department regarding this matter. In connection with fish traps my hon. friend stated that the minister refused to discuss the petitions which were presented by him to the house and which he alleged contained the signatures of ten thousand people. This matter was referred last year to the committee on fisheries and every opportunity was given to those who wanted to get information to obtain what they wanted. That committee made recommendations to this house which were implemented in full by the department. When the petitions were presented to the house by the hon member for Comox-Alberni, I raised no objection as it was not my duty to pass upon them or to state what should be done. Some petitions containing the same heading were forwarded to my office, I suppose inadvertently. These contained the postal addresses and occupations of the people who signed them and I found that they contained the signatures of more chicken farmers than fishermen.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Certainly. The fisherman
population is quite small as compared with the total population of British Columbia, and it will be still smaller if these traps are permitted.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is not true when the hon. member says that the minister refused to discuss the matter referred to in the petitions.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have the letter here.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The letter does not say that I refused.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Here is the letter.

Supply-Finance

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member read it?

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wrote to the minister on February 28, 1938, in connection with these petitions, and I said in part:
Are you disposed to give them notice that they will not be allowed any for or beyond this year, or do you propose to refer it again to the fishery committee of the house?
The answer was dated March 4, and reads:
Replying to your letter of the 28th ultimo with reference to the question of fish traps at Sooke, B.C., I beg to state that at the present time I am not disposed to give any notice that traps will not be allowed in the future. Further, I do not think that the petitions presented to the house should be referred to the fisheries committee inasmuch as they do not appear to disclose any new arguments besides those which were brought before the committee last year and inquired into.
I did not ask that the petitions should be referred to the committee; I asked that the data which the committee recommended last year should be gathered should be referred to it. I have that in my hand and I ask that it be referred to the committee.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is a matter which my hon. friend should refer either to the house or to the committee. As far as the department is concerned, the recommendations made last year by the committee were carried out. I feel that is all that should be expected of the minister or the department.
Regarding the other matter that was brought up, the wholesale destruction of fish by Japanese outside the three mile limit, I am sure my hon. friend knows that is an extremely delicate international matter. He must know that matter is being taken up by the United States and Canadian governments.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not know that.

maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend should have enough confidence in the government to know that matters of such importance will be considered as they should be considered. That is a matter Which can be remedied only by international treaties or agreements.
My hon. friend referred to the handing over of the jurisdiction over fisheries in non-tidal waters in British Columbia. I do not think he quite understands the situation. We have no jurisdiction to hand over anything that does not belong to us. What we did was to discontinue the administration of the sports fisheries in British Columbia. This was done because of recommendations made by representatives of the provincial government and officials of the department. We handed over all facilities that had been developed in that
respect. The exact limit of jurisdiction is a moot question and has been such ever since British Columbia entered confederation. Case after case has been submitted to the privy council and neither party has seemed to be satisfied with the decisions. However, I believe we have come to some understanding as to where the jurisdiction should end, and I think *the regulations have been amended so that they will meet with the approval of the provincial authorities. I shall deal with advertising later on when the appropriation for that service comes before the committee.
I was not given any notice of this matter, but I should like to say that when the items of the department come up for consideration I shall provide all the information in the possession of the department. I shall do my best to satisfy my hon. friend.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERIES-STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the Minister of Fisheries is dealing with his estimates, I would ask him to have available the necessary information to enable him to give the names and addresses of the persons concerned and the amounts received in connection with the appropriation of half a million dollars that was made last year and that was stated to be of great urgency to assist the distressed fishermen of Canada. I understand also that a report is being prepared in connection with possible markets for fish in South America and some parts of the West Indies, and I should like to feel that that report was before us before we consider further the matter involved in that expenditure, or in any expenditure which may be provided for in the estimates dealing with market conditions and the marketing of fish products.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
Departmental administration, $218,080.

There are a few questions that might be asked with respect to this item. What additions have been made to the departmental staff since the year ended March 31, 1937? I know there are three, but for what purpose have the additions been made? While it does not arise directly out of this item I will ask now, because it will enable the minister to give me the information later. What are the net proceeds of the last guaranteed Canadian National loan and what was the disposition made of the funds? The minister will remember that no information was given the house or the committee as to how the proceeds were distributed. It
Supply-M iscellaneous

was said that it was for the purpose of reimbursing expenditures that had been made by the dominion government. Of course, it would have a direct effect on the budget itself, and before we reach that stage perhaps the minister at the appropriate moment could state what were the proceeds of the loan and its distribution.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): With respect to the first question, while I have not my documents before me, there has been very little if any change in the departmental staff under this vote. The amount of increase is just sufficient to take care of the statutory increases in salaries. Any changes that I can at the moment recall are with respect to other votes, such as housing and so forth, and do not relate to this departmental administrative vote. The increase in the vote is some $6,000, and my right hon. friend will understand there could not be an increase in the staff for such a small amount.
With respect to the other question I shall be pleased to bring down the details at the appropriate time. I shall not attempt to do so now.
I would not expect them to-night.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is better to be accurate about a matter of that kind.

There is one other point. I assume that the entire finance department staff that formerly dealt with matters connected with currency is now part of the staff of the Bank of Canada, although they are housed as yet in part, until the new building is completed, in the finance department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
And the work of signing bills still goes on in the finance department, but as a matter of fact it is done for the Bank of Canada. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; that is correct.
I just wanted to be sure because I was asked that question the other day.
What is this item of express on coin shipments? There is a considerable increase.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend will be good enough to reserve his question until that vote is called, we shall have the information. The only vote I am calling to-night is the one relating to departmental administration.
Item agreed to.
Departmental administration, $137,145.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is exactly the same amount as last year except for an increase of $5,000 odd for the restoration of the salary deduction.

This would be the appropriate item under which to discuss the whole question of the administration of the Department of Justice, but it will serve my purpose if the minister is in a position to state when we may expect the report of the penitentiary commission. It is a document that will take some time to consider carefully, and I was hoping that it might be in our hands a reasonable time before the penitentiary estimates are considered.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. As a matter of fact the report is now complete and is in the hands of the translators and printers. I expect to be able to table it in the early future.
Thank you.

In regard to the act commonly known as the padlock law, I understand that the date for review is July 7. Will the minister be good enough to say when the government will come to a decision as to whether it is to be referred to the courts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The decision will be reached at the appropriate time. I shall have to work pretty hard on it because, as my hon. friend says, there is not much time left for study and consideration of such an important matter. But the decision will be reached in good time.
These philosophical cogitations and disputations that are so essential to determine the validity of the padlock law must necessarily involve a good deal of consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A good deal.
Item agreed to.

Elections and Franchise

speechtext: There is just one questioi which arises out of the consideration of that item, and that is as to there being a congestion of work in the patent office, which some have alleged is so serious as really to invite public criticism. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP THE SECRETARY OF STATE
